A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FlowDAS and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Retained experiments and relocated material can be reliably matched despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original Lorenz, Navier–Stokes, synthetic PIV, and double-well experiments, including quantitative results and appendix analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds SEVIR weather experiments, neural-operator comparisons, and a backbone ablation.

M1.justification: v2 extends single-state conditioning to histories of previous states, including ten states for Navier–Stokes and six for weather (Section 3.2). It also implements FNO and Transolver drift-model variants, using FNO for SEVIR. These substantially extend the model inputs and architectures while retaining the observation-guided stochastic-interpolant core.

E1.justification: Section 4.3 adds real SEVIR storm imagery, reconstructing future precipitation fields from previous frames and sparse current observations. This extends v1’s simulation-based coverage to real meteorological data. Lorenz, double-well, Navier–Stokes, and synthetic PIV remain; PIV is relocated to Appendix D.4.

E2.justification: Navier–Stokes comparisons expand from SDA alone to SDA, FNO-DA, and Transolver-DA (Table 2). The new neural-operator baselines incorporate observation-consistency optimization and also participate in weather comparisons. Lorenz and double-well retain SDA and BPF; PIV retains SDA.

E3.justification: For Navier–Stokes, SDA’s stated window changes from two to eleven, FlowDAS uses ten conditioning states, and FlowDAS training changes from 10,000 to 1,000 epochs. Weather introduces six-frame conditioning, 10% observations, next-frame and multi-step evaluation, and CSI metrics. These are reported protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish whether retained numerical results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a targeted weather-backbone ablation (Table S.11) and qualitative rollout examples, and extends the kinetic-energy analysis to neural operators. It removes v1’s PIV error-map analysis. The Monte Carlo sample-count, biased-versus-unbiased, integrator-order, and Lorenz forecasting analyses remain.

E5.justification: Weather Table 3 introduces means and standard deviations over unspecified multiple runs; Table S.11 also reports means with uncertainty values. Seeds and run counts are not supplied. Conversely, v1’s explicit disclosure of ten independent PIV results disappears. Increased repetitions of retained experiments are not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds neural-operator scores to Table 2, weather results to Table 3, and backbone results to Table S.11, and revises spectral curves. Weather RMSE is 0.053±0.004 for FlowDAS versus 0.062±0.001 for Transolver-DA. Lorenz and original ablation numbers remain unchanged. PIV’s 0.118/0.154 values are consistent with v1’s rounded 0.12/0.15, rather than demonstrated performance changes.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds a Stein-based drift–score derivation and definitions of lambda_s and c_s, absent in v1; most other derivations are relocated. Sampler expressions add X0, and process noise is no longer assumed Gaussian. The new lambda_s definition omits the factor -1/(sqrt(s) sigma_s) required by equations (S.17)–(S.19).

C1.justification: v2 broadens its main claims to superiority over neural operators and applicability to real weather with unavailable governing dynamics. The introduction also explicitly claims faster training than long-horizon diffusion bridges. These extend v1’s simulation/PIV-centered claims about assimilation accuracy, stability, and interpretability.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets history conditioning as enabling non-Markovian dynamics and contrasts observation-consistent probabilistic ensembles with deterministic neural forecasts requiring subsequent optimization. It adds interpretations of weather reconstruction and backbone performance. Earlier explanations concerning proximal initialization, rare events, and integration accuracy largely remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds code-access information, neural-operator and drift-backbone specifications, observation-update optimizer details, weighting parameters in Tables S.8–S.9, and weather inference parameters. However, v1’s explicit interpolation schedule and Navier–Stokes SDA training-epoch count are omitted. Reproducibility documentation is substantially expanded but also loses specific settings.

R1.justification: Related work expands from an emphasis on particle filters and SDA to neural operators, probabilistic surrogates, conditional diffusion bridges, and neural weather assimilation. New references include FNO, Transolver, FNP, FuXi-DA, and conditional video-prediction work. Several earlier inverse-problem references are removed, substantially changing the research positioning.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and method narrative are extensively revised. Methods are organized around three challenges; derivations and algorithms move into Appendices A–B. Existing appendices are reorganized, and weather replaces PIV as Section 4.3 while PIV moves to Appendix D.4.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces its result panel with guidance geometry. Figure 3 and the spectral plots are redesigned to include operator comparisons. Earlier Navier–Stokes panels are separated or relocated, PIV figures move to the appendix, and its error-map figure is removed. Weather figures, result tables, and baseline-parameter tables are added.

improvement.justification: SEVIR evaluation and neural-operator comparisons provide useful evidence beyond v1’s simulated demonstrations and SDA-only high-dimensional comparisons. Backbone analysis, uncertainty reporting, and clearer organization further improve assessment of the method. The net gain is limited by missing interpolation and run details and the coefficient inconsistency introduced in Appendix A.2, which weaken reproducibility and mathematical rigor.
